title: Choose NihonSub’s visual direction
question: The cinema-first layout is locked. Which visual language should carry it across the subtitler and A/B pages?

options.label: Program guide timecode
options.thesis: Make the shared video time the clearest visual thread through every subtitle comparison.
options.viewport: Every saved test remains selectable; its what-and-why summary leads into the wide player, with A above, B below, and the shared time marker continuing into both transcript tracks.
options.risk: The time-led cues could read like a schedule; keep standard app navigation and let the video remain the main surface.

raised.raise: Registration marks now tie the active video moment to both transcript tracks without adding a second layout system.
Long cue text stays readable in place instead of being cut to fit a media frame.

options.label: Cinema caption craft
options.lineage: Japanese cinema subtitle and title-card practice
options.thesis: Give each version a stable, legible position over the same moving image.
options.viewport: Every saved experiment remains selectable with its test summary; the selected run opens in a widescreen player with A above, B below, and the full transcript following.
options.risk: Theatrical styling can become generic cinema chrome; keep the controls and experiment list plainly usable.

options.label: Reference-setting rail
options.lineage: Wide-margin reference editions with a keyed center rail
options.thesis: Let one shared time rail register both versions against the video.
options.viewport: The cinema-first player stays dominant; below it, A and B transcript columns flank a narrow timecode rail.
options.case: The keyed rail makes timing and cue correspondence unusually clear; the print-reference world is less native to the user's media workflow.
options.risk: Small serif text and dense annotations could slow subtitle reading.

options.label: Variable type specimen
options.thesis: Use large type contrast to separate test names, subtitle copy, and timecodes.
options.viewport: The assigned player and transcript stay in place; typography carries hierarchy across the screen.
options.case: Typography is not the user's task, so a live specimen would obscure the subtitle work.
options.kept: Keep a strong scale distinction between experiment title, subtitle copy, and timecode.
options.risk: Typography tooling would make the app feel like a font editor.

options.label: Registration plate
options.thesis: Treat each active cue like a proof registered to its video moment.
options.viewport: Use small alignment marks at the current playhead while the player and transcript remain conventional app regions.
options.case: The marks clarify alignment but the annual's editorial world adds little recognition for a personal subtitling tool.
options.kept: Retain one functional registration mark at the shared playhead.
options.risk: Decorative crop marks would add noise around subtitles.

options.label: Ticket-wallet journey
options.lineage: Jet-age coupon wallets and baggage tags
options.thesis: Give each saved experiment a distinct identity and status.
options.viewport: The same player remains primary; restrained status marks distinguish saved A/B tests.
options.case: Run status can be clear, but coupon sequencing does not match how the user reviews subtitles.
options.kept: Keep experiment status and before/after labels explicit.
options.risk: Literal ticket shapes would turn functional controls into props.

options.label: Constructed type grid
options.thesis: Use a strict alignment grid to keep cue rows readable and stable.
options.viewport: The selected video and below-player transcript stay intact; a quiet grid disciplines the data.
options.case: A visible construction grid would compete with video and subtitle text.
options.kept: Maintain exact shared alignment for timestamps and cue rows.
options.risk: A visible grid can reduce contrast and make the screen feel technical for its own sake.

options.label: Vertical video feed
options.thesis: Let video occupy the screen and keep captions close to the image.
options.viewport: The cinema-first player remains landscape, with the transcript and experiment rationale available below.
options.case: The user needs landscape playback, two simultaneous tracks, and a readable transcript rather than feed navigation.
options.kept: Keep caption copy readable and expandable without truncation.
options.risk: A vertical-feed interaction would fight the current comparison task and longer-form video goal.

canonCard.label: The category standard
canonCard.thesis: Use a clear, neutral video-review interface with ordinary controls and no historical visual metaphor.
canonCard.viewport: A compact experiment summary sits above the wide player; two labeled transcript tracks follow below.
canonCard.risk: Familiar and clear, but visually less distinctive.
